title: Layers of the anterior abdominal wall
summary: Skin to peritoneum, and the arcuate line that changes everything below it.

steps.title: Start intact and peel
steps.text:
The wall is a sandwich: skin, Camper's fatty and Scarpa's membranous fascia, three flat muscles with their aponeuroses, transversalis fascia, extraperitoneal fat, peritoneum.

Use the dissection slider on the View tab to take it apart yourself – that is exactly the order a scalpel meets them in.

steps.title: External oblique
steps.text: Fibres run downwards and forwards – hands-in-pockets. Its aponeurosis forms the anterior rectus sheath and its lower free border rolls back on itself as the inguinal ligament.

check.q: Which way do the fibres of external oblique run?
check.a: Downwards and forwards — hands-in-pockets.

steps.title: Internal oblique and transversus
steps.text:
Internal oblique fibres run upwards and forwards, at right angles to external oblique; transversus abdominis runs horizontally. Three layers pulling in three directions is what makes the wall strong in every plane.

Their lower fibres arch over the spermatic cord to form the conjoint tendon.

check.q: Which layer do the segmental nerves of the abdominal wall run in?
check.a: Between internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

steps.title: Rectus abdominis and the arcuate line
steps.text:
Above the arcuate line (about midway between umbilicus and pubis) the internal oblique aponeurosis splits to pass in front of and behind rectus. Below it, all three aponeuroses pass in front, so the posterior sheath is absent and rectus lies directly on transversalis fascia.

That is why the inferior epigastric artery is easy to injure at a low port site, and why a Spigelian hernia appears at the lateral border of rectus near that line.

check.q: What changes at the arcuate line?
check.a: Below it all three aponeuroses pass in front of rectus abdominis, leaving only transversalis fascia behind.

steps.title: The blood supply and the section
steps.text:
Superior epigastric (from internal thoracic) and inferior epigastric (from external iliac) anastomose inside the rectus sheath – a potential collateral route in coarctation.

A transverse section makes the layers obvious; the labels show what the cut passes through.

check.q: Which two arteries anastomose within the rectus sheath?
check.a: The superior epigastric (from the internal thoracic) and the inferior epigastric (from the external iliac).

steps.title: The nerves travel between the deeper two layers
steps.text:
The main neurovascular plane of the anterolateral abdominal wall lies between internal oblique and transversus abdominis. Lower thoracic anterior rami continue from the intercostal spaces into this plane, giving branches to muscle and skin as they pass forwards.

Their terminal branches approach the rectus sheath and anterior abdominal skin. This arrangement links the wall to the segmental pattern of the thorax and explains why preserving muscle alone is not enough to preserve its function: a nerve can be interrupted in the layer beside it. Identify the two muscles enclosing the plane before tracing the nerve route.

check.q: Between which two muscle layers do the main thoracoabdominal nerves run?
check.a: Between internal oblique and transversus abdominis.

objectives: Name the layers of the anterior abdominal wall from skin to peritoneum
Describe the rectus sheath above and below the arcuate line
Explain the blood and nerve supply of the wall
Locate the main abdominal-wall neurovascular plane between internal oblique and transversus abdominis
takeaways: External oblique, internal oblique, transversus abdominis, then transversalis fascia.
Below the arcuate line all three aponeuroses pass in front of rectus.
Segmental nerves T7–L1 run between internal oblique and transversus.
Thoracoabdominal nerves travel mainly between internal oblique and transversus before supplying the muscles and skin of the anterior wall.

title: The inguinal canal
summary: Four walls, two rings, and how to tell a direct hernia from an indirect one.

steps.title: Why it exists
steps.text: An oblique 4 cm tunnel above the medial half of the inguinal ligament, left behind by the descent of the testis. It runs from the deep ring (a hole in transversalis fascia, half an inch above the mid-inguinal point) to the superficial ring (a triangular defect in the external oblique aponeurosis above the pubic tubercle).

steps.title: The four walls
steps.text:
Anterior: external oblique aponeurosis, plus internal oblique laterally.
Posterior: transversalis fascia, plus the conjoint tendon medially.
Roof: arching fibres of internal oblique and transversus.
Floor: the in-rolled inguinal ligament, plus the lacunar ligament medially.

Notice the design: the two weak points are reinforced by the opposite structure – MALT, two Muscles, two Aponeuroses, two Ligaments, two Transversalis layers.

check.q: What forms the posterior wall of the inguinal canal?
check.a: Transversalis fascia, reinforced medially by the conjoint tendon.

steps.title: Contents
steps.text:
In a man: the spermatic cord – three arteries (testicular, cremasteric, artery to the vas), three nerves (genital branch of genitofemoral, sympathetics, and the ilioinguinal on the cord rather than in it), three other things (vas, pampiniform plexus, lymphatics) and three coverings picked up on the way out.

In a woman: the round ligament of the uterus.

check.q: What are the contents of the inguinal canal in the male?
check.a: The spermatic cord and the ilio-inguinal nerve (which runs on the cord rather than through the deep ring).

steps.title: Direct versus indirect
steps.text:
The landmark is the inferior epigastric artery.

Indirect hernias enter the deep ring lateral to the artery, follow the cord and can reach the scrotum; a patent processus vaginalis can predispose to them, especially in children, while acquired factors also contribute in adults.
Direct hernias push through Hesselbach's triangle medial to the artery – bounded by the artery, the lateral border of rectus and the inguinal ligament – and rarely reach the scrotum.

check.q: How do you distinguish a direct from an indirect hernia at operation?
check.a: By its relation to the inferior epigastric vessels — indirect is lateral, direct is medial.

steps.title: The passage can carry fluid as well as bowel
steps.text:
During testicular descent, a peritoneal outpouching called the processus vaginalis accompanies the route through the inguinal canal. Its proximal connection normally closes, leaving the tunica vaginalis around part of the testis.

If that communication persists, peritoneal contents may enter through the deep ring. A passage admitting bowel or omentum can produce an indirect hernia; one mainly transmitting fluid can produce a communicating hydrocele. A patent passage is a predisposition, not a guarantee of symptoms, and adult indirect hernias can also involve acquired weakening.

check.q: What developmental connection is shared by an indirect hernia associated with a patent processus and a communicating hydrocele?
check.a: A persistent communication between the peritoneal cavity and the inguinal route through the processus vaginalis.

steps.title: The ilio-inguinal nerve joins partway along
steps.text:
The ilio-inguinal nerve traverses part of the inguinal canal and exits through the superficial ring. It does not enter through the deep ring with the spermatic cord. It pierces the muscular wall and joins the route farther along.

This is why a list of canal contents is not automatically a list of deep-ring contents. The genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve accompanies the cord through the deep ring, while the ilio-inguinal nerve takes its own entry. Both can be encountered in the region, but their paths and sensory territories are not identical.

check.q: Does the ilio-inguinal nerve enter the canal through the deep inguinal ring?
check.a: No. It enters through the muscular wall and traverses only part of the canal.

objectives: Give the boundaries of the inguinal canal
List its contents in the male and the female
Distinguish a direct from an indirect inguinal hernia
Relate a patent processus vaginalis to indirect hernia and communicating hydrocele
takeaways: Floor inguinal ligament, roof arching fibres, anterior external oblique, posterior transversalis fascia and conjoint tendon.
Indirect hernias pass through the deep ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
Direct hernias push through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to those vessels.
A persistent processus vaginalis provides a potential peritoneal route into the canal; its width and contents influence whether it presents as hernia or communicating hydrocele.

title: The diaphragm and its openings
summary: T8, T10, T12 – and why shoulder-tip pain means something under it.

steps.title: The muscle
steps.text: A musculotendinous dome with a sternal, a costal and a lumbar origin, all converging on a central tendon. It is the principal muscle of inspiration: as it descends the vertical dimension of the thorax increases and the lower ribs are levered outwards.

steps.title: Three openings
steps.text:
T8 – caval opening, in the central tendon: inferior vena cava and the right phrenic nerve. Being in the tendon, it is held open and widens on inspiration, which helps venous return.
T10 – oesophageal hiatus, in the right crus: oesophagus and the two vagal trunks. Muscular, so it pinches shut and acts as a sphincter.
T12 – aortic hiatus, behind the median arcuate ligament: aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein. It is behind rather than through the diaphragm, so aortic flow is unaffected by breathing.

I ate ten eggs at twelve.

check.q: Give the three main diaphragmatic openings and their levels.
check.a: Inferior vena cava at T8, oesophagus at T10, aorta at T12.

steps.title: The phrenic nerve
steps.text:
C3, 4 and 5 keep the diaphragm alive. The phrenic nerve supplies all its motor fibres and the sensation of the central part of both pleura and peritoneum.

Because those segments also supply the skin over the shoulder, irritation under the diaphragm – blood, a ruptured spleen, gas after laparoscopy – is felt as shoulder-tip pain.

check.q: Which nerve roots form the phrenic nerve?
check.a: C3, C4 and C5.

steps.title: The edge has a different sensory route
steps.text:
The phrenic nerve supplies the diaphragm's motor fibres and sensation from its central region and the adjacent central pleura and peritoneum. Sensation from the peripheral diaphragm travels mainly through lower intercostal and subcostal nerves.

That distinction affects where irritation is felt. Central diaphragmatic irritation may refer pain towards the shoulder through C3-C5 associations. Irritation nearer the costal attachment can be felt nearer the lower thoracic or upper abdominal wall. Shoulder-tip referral is therefore a useful central-diaphragm relationship, not the sensory map of every part of the muscle.

check.q: Which nerves carry most sensation from the peripheral diaphragm?
check.a: Lower intercostal and subcostal nerves; the phrenic nerve carries the central sensory supply.

steps.title: When one dome cannot pull down
steps.text:
During normal inspiration each hemidiaphragm contracts and descends. If one side loses its motor supply, it may sit higher because it no longer actively opposes pressure from the abdomen.

During a brisk inspiratory effort, the pressure change generated by the functioning respiratory muscles can pull the flaccid dome upwards instead of downwards. This is paradoxical movement. An elevated dome alone has several possible explanations, but opposite-direction movement illustrates what happens when a passive sheet replaces an actively contracting muscle.

check.q: Why might a paralysed hemidiaphragm rise during an inspiratory effort?
check.a: It cannot contract downwards, so pressure changes generated by the other muscles can displace the flaccid dome upwards.

objectives: Describe the attachments of the diaphragm
Name the three major openings and their levels and contents
Explain referred shoulder tip pain
Distinguish central phrenic sensation from peripheral intercostal sensation and explain paradoxical movement of a paralysed dome
takeaways: T8 caval, T10 oesophageal, T12 aortic — the numbers and the letters both increase.
The whole muscle is supplied by the phrenic nerve, C3–C5.
Central diaphragmatic irritation refers pain to the shoulder tip.
Central diaphragmatic sensation travels through the phrenic nerve; peripheral sensation uses lower intercostal and subcostal nerves. A paralysed dome may move upwards during inspiration.

title: The intercostal space
summary: Three muscle layers, one neurovascular bundle, and where to put the needle.

steps.title: Three layers again
steps.text:
External intercostal: fibres downwards and forwards, elevating the ribs in inspiration; membranous in front.
Internal intercostal: downwards and backwards; membranous behind.
Innermost intercostal: incomplete, and the neurovascular bundle runs between it and the internal layer.

check.q: Name the three muscle layers of an intercostal space.
check.a: External, internal and innermost intercostal muscles.

steps.title: VAN in the costal groove
steps.text:
From above downwards in the costal groove of the rib above: Vein, Artery, Nerve. Because the bundle hugs the lower border of the rib above, a needle or chest drain is passed just above the lower rib of the space.

Collateral branches run along the upper border of the lower rib, which is why 'just above' is a guide rather than a guarantee.

check.q: In what order do the vein, artery and nerve lie in the costal groove?
check.a: Vein, artery, nerve — from above downwards.

steps.title: Safe triangle for a chest drain
steps.text: Bounded by the lateral border of pectoralis major, the lateral border of latissimus dorsi, a line above the horizontal level of the nipple, and the apex below the axilla. This keeps you away from the internal thoracic vessels in front, the long thoracic nerve behind, and the diaphragm below.

check.q: Where is the safe triangle for a chest drain?
check.a: Between the lateral border of pectoralis major, the lateral border of latissimus dorsi and the fifth intercostal space.

steps.title: A thoracic nerve can finish in the abdomen
steps.text:
An intercostal nerve is the anterior ramus of a thoracic spinal nerve. The lower intercostal nerves, T7-T11, continue beyond the costal margin into the abdominal wall and are then often called thoracoabdominal nerves. T12 runs below the last rib as the subcostal nerve.

They retain their segmental arrangement while supplying abdominal muscles and skin. This explains why a thoracic root problem may be felt along a band extending into the abdomen, and why the innervation of the chest and abdominal wall should be learned as a continuous pattern.

check.q: Which thoracic anterior rami continue into the abdominal wall as thoracoabdominal nerves?
check.a: T7-T11; T12 is the subcostal nerve.

steps.title: The space is fed from both ends
steps.text:
Most posterior intercostal arteries arise from the thoracic aorta; the upper two usually come through the supreme intercostal artery. Anterior intercostal arteries arise from the internal thoracic artery and, lower down, its musculophrenic branch.

Where anterior branches are present, they connect with the posterior supply around the chest wall. These links help explain collateral routes between subclavian and descending aortic circulations. The lowest spaces do not all share the same anterior supply, so a general diagram should not be read as an identical branching pattern at every rib.

check.q: Which artery supplies the anterior intercostal branches of the upper spaces?
check.a: The internal thoracic artery.

objectives: Name the three muscle layers of an intercostal space
Describe the position of the neurovascular bundle
Justify where a needle or drain is inserted
Trace the continuation of lower intercostal nerves into the abdominal wall and the meeting of anterior and posterior intercostal arteries
takeaways: Vein, artery, nerve from above down in the costal groove.
The bundle runs between internal and innermost intercostal muscles.
Insert just above the lower rib to avoid the bundle.
T7-T11 anterior rami continue into the abdominal wall; intercostal arterial supply connects anterior and posterior routes within the spaces.

title: The mediastinum
summary: Divisions, and what crosses the sternal angle.

steps.title: The plane of Louis
steps.text: A line from the sternal angle to the lower border of T4 divides superior from inferior mediastinum. At that level: the arch of the aorta begins and ends, the trachea bifurcates, the azygos vein arches over the right bronchus, the thoracic duct crosses to the left, and the pulmonary trunk divides.

check.q: Name three things that happen at the level of the sternal angle.
check.a: The arch of the aorta begins and ends, the trachea divides at the carina, and it is the T4/5 disc level.

steps.title: Anterior, middle, posterior
steps.text:
Anterior: thymus, fat, lymph nodes – the usual home of a thymoma or retrosternal goitre.
Middle: heart in its pericardium, the roots of the great vessels, the phrenic nerves.
Posterior: descending aorta, oesophagus, thoracic duct, azygos system, sympathetic chains and the vagi.

check.q: What lies in the middle mediastinum?
check.a: The pericardium, the heart, the roots of the great vessels and the phrenic nerves.

steps.title: See it in section
steps.text: A transverse cut at the sternal angle is worth more than a paragraph. The labels name everything the plane passes through; click any of them to select it.

steps.title: In front of the root or behind it?
steps.text:
The phrenic nerve descends on the fibrous pericardium, between it and the mediastinal pleura, passing anterior to the root of the lung. Its destination is the diaphragm, so its course continues towards the inferior thorax.

The vagus passes posterior to the lung root and contributes to the oesophageal plexus before continuing as vagal trunks into the abdomen. This simple front-and-back relationship distinguishes two nerves that otherwise both descend through the chest. Use the hilum as the landmark instead of relying on how a nerve looks.

check.q: Which nerve passes anterior to a lung root, and which passes posterior?
check.a: Phrenic anterior; vagus posterior.

steps.title: The pericardium is tied to its neighbours
steps.text:
The fibrous pericardium is attached inferiorly to the central tendon of the diaphragm and blends superiorly with the connective tissue around the great vessels. It gives the heart a relatively fixed position while allowing movement within the serous-lined sac.

The serous pericardial layers enclose a small lubricated cavity, distinct from both pleural cavities. A collection within that cavity acts on the heart directly; fluid in a pleural cavity primarily affects the lung beside it. Middle mediastinum is a location, while pericardial cavity names a particular enclosed space within it.

The pericardium model shows the fibrous sac on the diaphragm below and blending into the great vessels above, with the serous layers folding back inside it.

check.q: Is the pericardial cavity continuous with either pleural cavity in normal anatomy?
check.a: No. The pericardial and pleural cavities are separate serous spaces.

steps.micro_view: Pericardium: The heart in its pericardium

objectives: Divide the mediastinum into its parts
List what lies in each division
Say what happens at the plane of the sternal angle
Use the lung root to distinguish phrenic from vagal routes and relate the pericardium to its neighbours
takeaways: Superior mediastinum above the sternal angle; anterior, middle and posterior below it.
The middle mediastinum is the pericardium and its contents.
The sternal angle plane marks the arch of the aorta, the carina and T4/5.
Phrenic nerves pass anterior to the lung roots on the pericardium; vagal nerves pass posterior to the roots towards the oesophageal plexus.

title: The vertebral column
summary: Regional differences you can identify on sight, and where the cord ends.

steps.title: Curves and regions
steps.text: Two primary (thoracic, sacral) kyphoses present from birth; two secondary (cervical, lumbar) lordoses that appear with holding the head up and walking. 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, 4 coccygeal.

check.q: Which curves of the spine are present at birth?
check.a: The thoracic and sacral (primary) curves.

steps.title: Atlas and axis
steps.text: C1 (atlas) has no body and no spine – a ring that carries the skull and allows nodding at the atlanto-occipital joints. C2 (axis) carries the dens, held against the anterior arch of the atlas by the transverse ligament; rotation happens here. Rupture of that ligament, or a dens fracture, threatens the cord at the level that also runs the diaphragm.

check.q: Which joint provides most of the rotation of the head?
check.a: The atlanto-axial joint, around the dens.

steps.title: Lumbar puncture
steps.text:
The spinal cord ends at about L1/L2 in an adult (L3 in a newborn), but the dural sac continues to S2. A needle entered at L3/L4 or L4/L5 – the level of the highest points of the iliac crests, Tuffier's line – meets only the cauda equina, whose roots float aside.

Layers pierced: skin, superficial fascia, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamentum flavum, epidural fat and veins, dura, arachnoid.

check.q: Which interspace is used for a lumbar puncture and why?
check.a: L3/4 or L4/5 — below the end of the cord at L1/L2, using the iliac crests (L4) as the landmark.

steps.title: Eight cervical nerves, seven cervical vertebrae
steps.text:
The first seven cervical spinal nerves leave above the correspondingly numbered vertebrae. The extra C8 nerve leaves between C7 and T1. From T1 downwards, spinal nerves leave below the vertebra of the same number.

This change in numbering is separate from the difference between spinal cord segments and vertebral levels. The lower cord segments lie well above their eventual bony exits, so their roots descend within the canal. Always specify whether a number labels a vertebra, a disc, a cord segment or a nerve root.

check.q: Where does the C8 spinal nerve leave the vertebral canal?
check.a: Between C7 and T1, below C7 and above T1.

steps.title: The root passing by is not the root leaving
steps.text:
At the L4-L5 disc, the L4 root is the exiting root in the intervertebral foramen. The L5 root is still travelling down inside the canal towards its lower exit. A usual posterolateral disc herniation therefore tends to compress the traversing L5 root.

A far-lateral or foraminal herniation at the same disc level can instead affect the exiting L4 root. The disc label alone does not fully identify the injured nerve; the position of the herniation relative to the two routes matters. Picture the roots descending before selecting the level.

check.q: Which root is commonly affected by a posterolateral L4-L5 disc herniation, and which by a far-lateral one?
check.a: The traversing L5 root in the usual posterolateral pattern; the exiting L4 root in the far-lateral pattern.

objectives: Identify a vertebra by region on sight
Describe the normal curves and when each appears
State where the cord ends and the practical consequence
Explain cervical spinal nerve numbering and distinguish exiting from traversing lumbar roots
takeaways: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, then sacrum and coccyx.
Cervical vertebrae have foramina transversaria; thoracic have costal facets; lumbar are massive.
The cord ends at L1/L2, so lumbar puncture is done below that.
C1-C7 nerves exit above their matching vertebrae, C8 exits between C7 and T1, and lower nerves exit below. A typical L4-L5 posterolateral disc herniation affects the traversing L5 root.
